title: In Their Own Words
sub: Grades 5–8 · ELA · Diaries, testimony and quotation in context

hero.credit: Ted Eytan, *Holocaust Day*. CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

objective: Students will read the words of young people who wrote during the Holocaust — Anne and Margot Frank, Elsa Binder — beside the testimony of people who remembered it later, as the exhibition sets them in *A Minute’s Stillness* and on its posters. They will tell a **diary** written at the time from **testimony** remembered later, read each passage closely for who, when, where and what it reveals, and write a **remembrance label** that quotes exactly and gives the words their context.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The people of the Holocaust are remembered best in their own words. Reading those words closely, and quoting them honestly, is how we keep faith with the people who wrote them.

materials: *The words in this lesson* on page 3, projected or printed
Differentiated handouts, one per student; *A Minute’s Stillness* on a screen if you have one
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** *A Minute’s Stillness* shows, one at a time, a name, a writer’s words, and a question to sit with; each minute is different. The second poster’s *Children* chapter tells Anne Frank’s story; *Lay a Stone* is a place to end.

steps.title: Who wrote this?
script: Project the sentence without a name. *“Read it twice. Who might have written this, and where? What does writing do for the writer?”* Take guesses. Then: it was written by a girl in hiding with her family, in rooms behind a bookcase in her father’s office building in Amsterdam. Her name was Anne Frank, and she dreamed of being a writer.

screen.text: “When I write I can shake off all my cares. My sorrow disappears, my spirits are revived!”

steps.purpose: Meet the words before the name: let students wonder who wrote them, and why.
students: Read it twice. Who might have written this?
What does writing do for the writer?

steps.title: Young writers
script: Show the young writers *A Minute’s Stillness* names (page 3). Anne Frank was not alone: Petr Ginz kept a diary in Theresienstadt, Yitskhok Rudashevski in the Vilna ghetto, Dawid Sierakowiak in five notebooks in the Łódź ghetto, and Moshe Flinker wrote about his faith while hiding his identity in Belgium.

screen.caption: Young writers in A Minute’s Stillness, as the exhibition describes them

steps.purpose: See that Anne Frank was one of many young people who kept writing.
students: What did each one hope for, or hold on to?

steps.title: Then, or later?
script: Set out the two kinds of source. A **diary** or a letter is written at the time, without knowing what will happen next. **Testimony** is remembered later, by someone who survived and looks back. Read the four voices and sort them: Elsa Binder and Margot Frank wrote then; Ann Kirk and Bea Green remember the Kindertransport, which brought about 10,000 children to safety in Britain.

screen.caption: Four voices: which were written at the time, and which remembered later?

cells: “Everything comes to an end. Spring will come.”
Elsa Binder, aged 22, writing in the Stanisławów ghetto
“We, however, pretended I was going on a marvellous adventure.”
Ann Kirk, who left Berlin on the Kindertransport aged 10
“We never feel safe, because we border directly on Germany and we are only a small country.”
Margot Frank, in a letter to a pen pal in America, 1940
“I said, you’ll see her again soon. I was really talking to myself.”
Bea Green, 14, comforting a younger girl on the Kindertransport train

steps.purpose: Tell a diary or letter written at the time from testimony remembered later.
students: Which were written at the time?
Which were remembered later? What gives it away?

steps.title: In context
script: Show Anne’s words of July 15, 1944. The Anne Frank House warns that the first sentence has been *“plucked out of context”*, so the exhibition never shows it alone: the sentence that follows it always comes too. Ask what the second sentence adds.

screen.text:
“I still believe, in spite of everything, that people are truly good at heart.”
“And yet, when I look up at the sky, I somehow feel that everything will change for the better, that this cruelty, too, shall end, that peace and tranquility will return once more.”

steps.purpose: See how the sentence around a quotation changes what it means.
students: What does the second sentence add to the first?
Why would a museum never show the first one alone?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels read the same voices and end in a remembrance label.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read four short passages with a guide: who, when, and one word that shows a feeling. Sort them into *written then* and *remembered later*, then complete a remembrance card with sentence frames.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Close-read four voices in a chart, explain what a diary can show that testimony cannot (and the other way), then write a 60–80 word remembrance label that quotes exactly.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh two quotations the exhibition handles with care — Anne Frank’s words of July 15, 1944, and Martin Niemöller’s *First They Came* — then argue what a writer owes the words they quote, and write a label.

steps.purpose: Read and write about the writers’ words at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three levels read the same voices.

steps.title: Bear witness
script: Ask three students to read their labels aloud, one after another, without comment. Then read Elie Wiesel’s words: *“For the dead and the living, we must bear witness.”* Ask: *how did your label bear witness?*

screen.text: “For the dead and the living, we must bear witness.”
screen.cite: Elie Wiesel, who survived Auschwitz and Buchenwald

steps.purpose: Hear the labels read aloud, as a way of bearing witness.
students: Read your label aloud: the name, the words, the context.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
